result: Basalin is essential for basal plate formation in trypanosomes. RNAi ablation of basalin results in the absence or severe reduction of the basal plate structure at the transition zone, as demonstrated by TEM analysis showing 57% of longitudinal sections lacking a visible basal plate and 33% having a greatly reduced basal plate after 48 hours of RNAi.
evaluation: Claims C5, C33, C61, C64, and C70 collectively demonstrate through localization data (C66-C67) and TEM evidence (C61) that basalin is required for basal plate formation. The correlation between basalin ablation and basal plate absence is well-documented with quantitative TEM data.

result: Loss of basalin causes central pair nucleation defects in trypanosomes. After basalin RNAi, 68% of axoneme cross-sections lack both CP microtubules and 20% lack one CP microtubule. PF16 (a CP marker) is absent in 63% of single-flagellum cells and 97% of early new flagella, with increasing incorporation at later cell cycle stages, indicating delayed and inefficient CP nucleation.
evaluation: Claims C6, C32, C47, C54-C60 provide converging evidence from TEM (C54-C55) and fluorescence microscopy (C47, C56-C57) demonstrating CP defects. The temporal analysis of PF16 incorporation (C56-C60) strongly supports a nucleation defect rather than a stability defect, as argued in C125 and C127.

result: Basalin ablation causes flagellum paralysis in trypanosomes. Video microscopy demonstrates that flagella of basalin RNAi-induced cells are immotile.
evaluation: Claims C8, C31, and C40 are supported by video evidence (Video 1) showing paralyzed flagella after basalin RNAi. This phenotype is consistent with the CP defects observed (C6, C32) since the CP is known to coordinate flagellar beating.

result: Basalin is required for efficient recruitment of TZP103.8 to the transition zone. When basalin is ablated by RNAi, TZP103.8 becomes undetectable or almost undetectable at the TZ by fluorescence microscopy, while basalin recruitment is unaffected when TZP103.8 is ablated.
evaluation: Claims C7, C71, and C128 are supported by two-color fluorescence microscopy data (Figure 5) showing the hierarchical dependency between basalin and TZP103.8. The reciprocal experiment (C72) confirms basalin acts upstream of TZP103.8 in the assembly pathway.

result: LmxM.22.1070 is a highly divergent syntenic ortholog of basalin in Leishmania mexicana. Despite extremely weak BLASTP homology (e=0.27 and 1.9), LmxM.22.1070 occupies the syntenic locus, localizes to the basal body/pro-basal body, and its knockout reproduces the missing basal plate phenotype observed in trypanosome basalin RNAi.
evaluation: Claims C9, C35-C36, C94-C95, C97-C98, C103, C113, and C121 provide multiple lines of evidence (synteny, localization, functional phenotype) demonstrating orthology despite extreme sequence divergence. The combination of genomic synteny (C94-C95), similar localization (C103), and identical loss-of-function phenotype (C36, C113) strongly supports the orthology claim.

result: Basalins are predicted to be ~65% intrinsically disordered proteins. Both TbBasalin and LmxBasalin show similar levels of predicted intrinsic disorder, and HHpred analysis suggests a conserved core helical scaffold that is plastic to insertions of disordered sequences. This high degree of disorder may explain the extreme sequence divergence and suggests basalin may function as a hub or scaffold protein.
evaluation: Claims C10, C102, and C169-C176 are supported by bioinformatics predictions (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 2). The ~65% disorder prediction is quantitative (C102), and the interpretation that this may facilitate protein-protein interactions (C11, C170-C172) is reasonable speculation grounded in established properties of intrinsically disordered proteins (C169-C173).

result: LmxM.22.1070 knockout in Leishmania mexicana shows CP defects similar to trypanosome basalin RNAi. The CP is absent from 41% of axonemal cross-sections, with 31% showing 9+2 and 10% showing 9+1 configurations. PF16 is either completely absent (40%) or partially missing (40%) from protruding flagella, with a more penetrant phenotype (90% PF16-negative) in non-protruding flagella.
evaluation: Claims C112, C117-C118, and C133-C135 are supported by TEM data (Figure 9) and fluorescence microscopy (Figure 10). The quantitative data on CP presence/absence and PF16 incorporation patterns are consistent with the trypanosome basalin phenotype, supporting functional conservation.

result: Basalin localizes to the expected position of the basal plate at the transition zone. Two-color fluorescence microscopy shows basalin is positioned ~100 nm more proximal than TZP103.8, corresponding to the basal plate location. Basalin signal is also detected at the pro-basal body and increases in intensity as the pro-basal body matures.
evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are supported by two-color fluorescence microscopy data (Figure 4). The localization is consistent with the expected position of the basal plate based on TZP103.8 as a reference marker, and the developmental pattern at the pro-basal body is well-documented.

result: Basalin ablation causes secondary morphological defects including shorter flagella (~9 μm reduction), supernumerary DNA-containing structures, reduced kinetoplast-nucleus distance, and increased free flagellum length. These defects are likely consequences of cell division defects caused by the shortened flagellum at cytokinesis.
evaluation: Claims C41-C46 are supported by quantitative microscopy data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The interpretation that these are secondary consequences of flagellar defects (C46) is reasonable and supported by citations to previous work on flagellum-dependent cytokinesis in trypanosomes.

result: Basalin ablation has differential effects on axonemal components. Hydin (C2 projection) signal becomes fainter and more punctate in 31% of cells but remains stably associated with the flagellum after detergent extraction. RSP2 (radial spokes) and dynein arm localization are unaffected, suggesting radial spokes and doublet microtubules are not significantly altered.
evaluation: Claims C48-C53 are supported by fluorescence microscopy data (Figure 1). The differential effects on CP components (PF16 absent, Hydin reduced) versus radial spokes and dynein (unaffected) indicate the defect is specific to CP assembly rather than general axonemal structure.

result: Gamma tubulin localizes ~400 nm proximal to basalin and TZP103.8 with no signal overlap. Basalin ablation causes a general reduction in gamma tubulin signal but does not prevent its recruitment to the basal body. Conversely, gamma tubulin ablation does not prevent recruitment of basalin or TZP103.8 to the TZ.
evaluation: Claims C78-C82, C84-C85, and C130 are supported by two-color fluorescence microscopy data (Figure 6). The mutual independence of recruitment demonstrates that basalin and gamma tubulin function in parallel or convergent pathways for CP assembly, as concluded in C131.

result: TZP103.8 RNAi results in lack of CP microtubules but does not cause disappearance of the basal plate, although electron density is somewhat reduced in 11/32 TZ longitudinal sections. This demonstrates that the lack of CP does not cause basal plate absence, supporting the conclusion that basalin acts upstream in basal plate formation.
evaluation: Claims C73-C75 and C132 are supported by TEM data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and citation to Dean et al., 2016. This reciprocal experiment is critical for establishing the causal relationship: basalin is required for basal plate formation, which in turn is required for efficient CP nucleation.

result: LmxM.22.1070 knockout cells in Leishmania mexicana are viable but show substantial morphological aberrations including strong motility defects, slower doubling times, substantially shorter flagella with most cells lacking a protruding flagellum, and shorter, rounder cell bodies. These morphological changes are consistent with the link between flagellum biogenesis and cell shape.
evaluation: Claims C104-C111 are supported by video evidence (Video 2), growth curves, and microscopy data (Figure 9—figure supplement 1). The phenotypes parallel those observed in trypanosome basalin RNAi, supporting functional conservation of the protein.

result: The morphological and growth defects of LmxM.22.1070 knockout are rescued by episomal expression of LmxM.22.1070 but not by T. brucei basalin, demonstrating some degree of biochemical divergence between the orthologs despite functional conservation.
evaluation: Claims C115-C116 and C177-C178 are supported by rescue experiment data (Figure 9—figure supplement 1). The species-specific rescue demonstrates that while the proteins are functionally orthologous, they have diverged sufficiently that cross-species complementation does not occur, consistent with the extreme sequence divergence observed.

result: In basalin-negative flagella, CP nucleation is delayed and occurs ectopically at low frequency in the distal axoneme. Early new flagella lack PF16, with probability of incorporation increasing in later stages, arguing for a nucleation defect rather than a stability defect. Some CP assembly (10-20%) occurs in the absence of the basal plate, possibly through stochastic self-assembly due to mis-localization of nucleating factors.
evaluation: Claims C125-C127 and C136-C138 provide a mechanistic interpretation of the temporal PF16 incorporation data. The reasoning that rules out the stability hypothesis (C127) is sound based on the observed temporal pattern. The interpretation of ectopic assembly (C137-C138) is reasonable speculation supported by the data and consistent with Chlamydomonas studies (C139).

result: Initial bioinformatics analyses suggested basalin has a highly restricted evolutionary distribution, not detected outside Trypanosoma species or even in Leishmania. Even in closely related T. congolense, the ortholog is highly divergent. This extreme divergence is more pronounced than other examples like the nuclear pore complex and suggests that the proportion of lineage-specific proteins in flagellar proteomes may be overestimated.
evaluation: Claims C86-C87, C34, C89, C168, C179, C183-C184 are supported by bioinformatics analysis using Orthofinder and BLASTP. The failure to detect orthologs using standard homology searches, combined with the subsequent discovery of a functional ortholog through synteny, demonstrates the limitations of sequence-based approaches for highly divergent proteins.

result: Kinetoplastid genomes are highly syntenic with genes arranged in directional gene clusters, and synteny is highly conserved even when there is extensive sequence divergence. This property was essential for discovering the basalin ortholog and represents one of the few groups of organisms where this type of syntenic genome analysis is possible.
evaluation: Claims C90-C92 and C181-C182 are supported by citations to Ghedin et al., 2004 and represent established knowledge about kinetoplastid genome organization. The importance of synteny for this discovery (C181) is well-demonstrated by the fact that sequence homology alone failed to identify the ortholog.

result: In L. mexicana parental cells, the basal plate delimits a clear border between the TZ and axoneme inner regions with different electron densities. In basalin KO cells, this border is lost with homogeneous electron density, suggesting a boundary function for the basal plate. However, axonemal structures do not penetrate into the TZ, suggesting the TZ/axoneme boundary remains intact.
evaluation: Claims C161-C166 are supported by TEM observations. The interpretation of a boundary function (C164) is reasonable speculation based on the electron density changes. The observation that axonemal structures don't penetrate the TZ (C165-C166) provides an important qualification to the boundary function hypothesis.

result: The authors propose that basalins may act as 'hubs' facilitating protein-protein interactions due to their high intrinsic disorder, and that basalin may be conserved in many organisms where it remains cryptic due to extreme sequence divergence. This raises the general concept that proteins appearing organism-specific may have highly divergent cryptic orthologs responsible for conserved functions.
evaluation: Claims C11, C38-C39, C122, C174-C175, and C180 represent speculative interpretations and generalizations from the basalin findings. While the speculation about hub function (C11) is reasonable given the intrinsic disorder, it lacks direct experimental evidence. The broader claims about cryptic orthologs in other organisms (C122, C180) are intriguing hypotheses but remain unproven without identification of basalin orthologs outside kinetoplastids.

result: The mechanism of gamma tubulin-mediated CP nucleation remains unclear. Gamma tubulin localizes ~400 nm proximal to the CP nucleation site. The authors discuss multiple possible models: direct nucleation at the basal plate, nucleation at a distance with basal plate capture, or a pre-assembly pool at the basal body. Comparisons with Chlamydomonas stellate structure suggest these structures may not be analogous.
evaluation: Claims C141-C155 represent a discussion of mechanistic possibilities rather than definitive conclusions. While gamma tubulin is established as essential for CP nucleation (C141, supported by citations), the spatial relationship and mechanism remain unclear (C142). The various models proposed (C151-C155) are reasonable speculations but lack direct experimental support in this study.

result: CP number control requires that exactly two CP microtubules are incorporated into the axoneme. Chlamydomonas mutants lacking radial spokes or with 10 doublets have 4 CP microtubules, suggesting space availability plays a role in limiting CP number. The absence of extra CPs in basalin mutants argues that CP number is still constrained.
evaluation: Claims C156-C160 are supported by citations to studies in Chlamydomonas (C157-C159) and observations from basalin mutants (C160). The reasoning about number control is sound, though the mechanism remains unclear. The observation that basalin mutants don't have extra CPs (C160) is an important constraint on models of CP assembly.

result: TZ structures such as the collarette remain after basalin RNAi. Basalin and TZP103.8 remain associated with isolated flagella even after extraction with near-saturating concentrations of salt, suggesting they are core structural components of TZ structures.
evaluation: Claims C62, C76, and C77 are supported by TEM observations (C62) and biochemical extraction experiments (C76). The resistance to high salt extraction (C76) supports the interpretation that these are core structural components (C77) rather than peripherally associated proteins.

result: Background claims about flagellar structure, CP function, and prior studies on CP assembly. These include established knowledge about the 9+2 axoneme structure, CP coordination of flagellar beating, disease associations, basal plate structure, and previous studies on gamma tubulin and katanin roles in CP assembly.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4 and C12-C30 represent established knowledge and prior work supported by appropriate citations. These provide necessary context for the current study but are not novel findings. The citations appear appropriate and the background information is accurately represented.

result: Bioinformatics characterization of basalin and LmxM.22.1070 shows that gene synteny is highly conserved between T. brucei and L. mexicana, LmxM.22.1070 is not a clear sequence homolog, most conserved residues lie in or near predicted helices, and neither protein contains conserved domains that could provide functional clues, though some coiled-coils and alpha helices were detected.
evaluation: Claims C93-C94, C96, C99-C101 are supported by bioinformatics analysis shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The synteny analysis (C94) and HHpred comparison (C99) provide the basis for identifying LmxM.22.1070 as a candidate ortholog despite weak sequence similarity (C96).

result: Short, non-protruding flagella in LmxM.22.1070 knockout cells may be 'newer' flagella that have had less time for stochastic ectopic assembly of PF16 and CP. Consistent with this, cells with two free flagella were not observed in KO cells, probably because the new flagellum remained short.
evaluation: Claims C119-C120 represent reasonable speculation based on the observation that short flagella have a more penetrant PF16-negative phenotype (C118). However, the interpretation that these are necessarily 'newer' flagella (C119) lacks direct temporal evidence. The observation about absence of two-flagellum cells (C120) is supported by data but the causal explanation is speculative.

result: The proportion of flagella lacking a basal plate correlates with the proportion of axoneme cross-sections lacking CP, and mutant analysis demonstrates the link between basal plate structure and CP assembly. Basalin is the first example of a protein required for basal plate formation, and complex pathways are involved in CP formation.
evaluation: Claims C63, C65, C123-C124, C131-C132 represent key conclusions from the study. The correlation between basal plate absence and CP defects (C63, C65) is supported by quantitative TEM data. The claim that basalin is the first basal plate protein (C123) is supported by the authors' knowledge of the literature. The conclusion about complex pathways (C131) is supported by the differential dependencies observed.

result: Studies in Chlamydomonas demonstrate that CP can self-assemble at different points along pre-formed flagella during cytoplasmic complementation of katanin mutants. Under normal conditions, the presence of a basal plate-located nucleating factor may facilitate assembly of a full CP running from basal plate to tip.
evaluation: Claim C139 is supported by citation to Lechtreck et al., 2013 and provides important context for interpreting the ectopic CP assembly observed in basalin mutants. Claim C140 is reasonable speculation about normal CP assembly based on the mutant phenotypes, though it lacks direct experimental support.

result: Background on intrinsically disordered proteins and comparison with other divergent protein families. Analysis of trypanosome NPC architecture suggested common ancestry with yeast and metazoan NPCs despite lack of sequence conservation, though basalin divergence is more extreme. Intrinsically disordered proteins associate with cytoskeletal elements and can function as hubs, scaffolds, or molecular glue, often with only a few conserved peptides.
evaluation: Claims C167 and C169-C173 represent established knowledge about intrinsically disordered proteins supported by appropriate citations. These provide important context for interpreting the basalin findings. The comparison with NPC divergence (C167-C168) helps calibrate the extreme nature of basalin sequence divergence.
